content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on carbohydrate intake for adults and children, which were accessed on May 25, 2023. These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for optimal carbohydrate consumption to promote health and prevent disease. Similarly, WHO has issued guidelines on total fat intake to prevent unhealthy weight gain in both adults and children. These recommendations, also accessed on May 25, 2023, emphasize the importance of maintaining a balanced fat intake to support overall health. WHO has further provided guidance on the intake of saturated fatty acids and trans-fatty acids for adults and children. These guidelines, accessed on May 25, 2023, aim to reduce the risk of cardiovascular diseases and other health complications associated with excessive consumption of these fats. The use of non-sugar sweeteners is addressed in another WHO guideline, which outlines their role in dietary practices and their potential health implications. WHO has also developed specific guidelines on sodium intake for adults and children, accessed on January 1, 2023. These recommendations focus on reducing sodium consumption to lower the risk of hypertension and related cardiovascular diseases. In addition, WHO has published guidelines on potassium intake for adults and children, accessed on January 1, 2023. These guidelines highlight the importance of adequate potassium consumption in maintaining healthy blood pressure levels and overall cardiovascular health. A study by de Ruyter et al., published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2012, investigated the effects of sugar-free versus sugar-sweetened beverages on body weight in children. The findings provide valuable insights into the role of sugar consumption in childhood obesity. Taljaard et al. conducted a randomized, double-blind, controlled intervention study in 2013, published in the British Journal of Nutrition. This study examined the effects of a multi-micronutrient-fortified beverage, with and without sugar, on growth and cognition in South African schoolchildren. Ventura and Worobey explored early influences on the development of food preferences in a 2013 article published in Current Biology. Their research sheds light on how early dietary exposures shape long-term food choices. De Cosmi, Scaglioni, and Agostoni discussed the impact of early taste experiences on later food choices in a 2017 article published in Nutrients. Their findings emphasize the importance of early dietary habits in shaping lifelong eating behaviors. Ariza et al. examined taste perception as a risk factor for childhood obesity in a 2018 article published in Salud Pública de México. This study, written in Spanish, highlights the role of taste preferences in the development of obesity in children. The Global Nutrition Policy Review 2016–2017, published by WHO, assessed country progress in creating enabling policy environments for promoting healthy diets and nutrition. This review, accessed on January 1, 2023, provides a comprehensive overview of global efforts to address malnutrition and diet-related health issues. Another WHO publication, Global Nutrition Policy Review: What Does It Take to Scale Up Nutrition Action? was accessed on January 1, 2023. This document outlines strategies for scaling up nutrition interventions to improve public health outcomes. The WHO Steering Group includes experts such as Dr. Ayoub Al-Jawaldeh, Dr. Anshu Banerjee, Dr. Hana Bekele, and others, who contribute their expertise in nutrition, public health, and related fields to guide the development of WHO guidelines. The guideline development group (NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health) comprises professionals with diverse expertise, including Professor Hayder Al-Domi, Professor John H. Cummings, Emeritus Professor Ibrahim Elmadfa, Dr. Lee Hooper, and others. Their areas of expertise range from human nutrition and dietetics to systematic review methods and public health nutrition. External peer reviewers, such as Professor Khaleda Islam, Dr. Yoona Kim, Dr. Amos Laar, and others, provide critical feedback on the guidelines to ensure their scientific rigor and relevance. Declarations of interest from members of the guideline development group were assessed to ensure transparency and avoid conflicts of interest. For example, Mary L’Abbé disclosed her involvement with various organizations, including the Iodine Global Network, WHO Collaborating Centre on Nutrition Policy, and others. These engagements were evaluated and determined not to pose a conflict of interest for her role in the guideline development process. Barbara Schneeman disclosed her previous roles with the US Agency for International Development (USAID), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and other organizations. Her engagements were similarly assessed and found not to conflict with her contributions to the guideline development process.
